appraisal_events.evidence: M. Swann was in fact one of the most elegant members of the Jockey-Club, the favorite friend of the comte de Paris and the prince de Galles, one of the most courted men in the fashionable society of the Faubourg Saint-Germain -- a brilliant life the family, with their bourgeois idea of fixed social castes, never suspected.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator sharply elevates Swann by revealing his real standing in the highest aristocratic society, a truth completely hidden from the unsuspecting bourgeois family who host him as an ordinary family friend.

appraisal_events.evidence: Ma grand'tante doubts Swann has any real connoisseurship ('vous devez vous faire repasser des croûtes'), calls him 'un vrai type' before company, publicly teases him in front of visitors about living near the wine warehouse to catch his train, and later dismisses Françoise's report that he dined with a princess as merely 'une princesse du demi-monde.'
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator shows the vulgar great-aunt repeatedly belittling Swann's taste and mocking his choices in front of visitors, then waving away evidence of his real prestige -- a diminishment the narration frames as her own ignorant vulgarity rather than an accurate verdict on Swann.

status_effects.explanation: Swann's true standing in elite aristocratic society is revealed as far higher than his hosts imagine, marking a clear elevation invisible within the family's own frame.

Within the family scene, the great-aunt openly doubts Swann's taste and mocks him as an eccentric curiosity, locally diminishing him even though the narration marks her judgment as vulgar and mistaken.

The great-aunt publicly needles Swann in front of visitors about his modest, eccentric quarter and dismisses the report that he dined with a princess, visibly undercutting his standing among those present even as the reader knows better.

ambiguities: The great-aunt's mockery of Swann's taste and quarter, and her dismissal of the report that he dined with a princess, is framed with narratorial irony that undercuts her judgment even as it stages a real local social diminishment within the family scene.
